Perpetua lifted Felicity from the ground, and the two exchanged the kiss of peace before being killed by the sword. Their names are in the Roman Canon of the Mass. Their memorial is celebrated on March 7.
joao-de-deus:
A boy who left home

John Cidade was born on March 8, 1495, in Montemor-o-Novo, Portugal. At eight years old, for reasons no one fully knows, he left home and ended up in Oropesa, Spain, where he grew up working as a shepherd for a farmer. As a young man he enlisted as a soldier and fought in the wars of Emperor Charles V, leading a dissolute life. Later he was a shepherd again, worked in North Africa helping an impoverished Portuguese family and finally became a seller of books and religious images in Granada, Spain.

The "madman" of Granada

Around 1537, when he was over forty, he heard a sermon by Saint John of Ávila and was so moved that he began crying out for God's mercy, tore up the books he sold, gave away everything he had and walked the streets weeping for his sins. The people thought he was mad, and he was confined in the royal hospital, where the mentally ill were treated with whippings. Saint John of Ávila visited him and helped him turn that fervor into service to those who suffered as he did.

"Do good, brothers"

In 1539 John rented a house in Granada and began taking in the poor sick, the abandoned and the homeless. At night he went through the streets with a basket on his back, begging alms and saying: "Do good to yourselves, brothers!" He himself washed, fed and cared for each patient, treating them with dignity. A bishop gave him the name by which he became known: John of God. During a fire at the royal hospital he went into the burning building several times and brought the patients out without being burned.

Patron of hospitals

In 1550, trying to save a young man drowning in the Genil River, he fell gravely ill. He died on March 8 of that year, his birthday, kneeling before a crucifix. His companions continued the work and formed the Hospitaller Order of Saint John of God, which today cares for the sick in dozens of countries. He was canonized in 1690 and is the patron of hospitals, the sick and nurses. His memorial is March 8.
francisca-romana:
A noble girl who wanted to be a nun

Frances was born in 1384 in Rome, into a noble and wealthy family. From childhood she prayed a great deal and wished to become a religious sister. But, as was the custom of the time, her parents arranged her marriage when she was only twelve, to Lorenzo Ponziani, a young Roman nobleman. Frances obeyed and was a devoted wife. The marriage, which lasted about forty years, was happy, and the couple had three children.

Wife, mother and servant of the poor

Together with her sister-in-law Vannozza, who became her great friend, Frances visited the hospitals and the poor of Rome, bringing food and clothing and caring for the sick. She is said to have taught that a married woman must sometimes leave God at the altar to find him in her household tasks. She lived through very hard times: Rome was invaded, the family palace was looted, her husband was wounded and her eldest son was even taken hostage. During an epidemic of plague and a great famine she lost two of her children, yet she turned her own home into a hospital and gave everything she had to those in need.

The guardian angel

Frances had a very deep life of prayer and received mystical graces. According to the accounts of her confessor, for many years she saw her guardian angel at her side, guiding her and, at night, lighting the way when she went out to help someone. For this reason, in 1925 Pope Pius XI declared her patron of motorists.

The Oblates of Tor de' Specchi

In 1425 Frances gathered a group of Roman women who wanted to serve God and the poor without leaving their families, and who later came to live in community: the Oblates of Mary, linked to the Olivetan Benedictine monks. After her husband's death in 1436, Frances went to live with them and became their superior. She died on March 9, 1440, and was canonized in 1608. She is the patron of Rome, of homemakers and of widows. Her memorial is March 9.
sao-patricio:
A slave in Ireland

Patrick was born around the year 385 in Roman Britain. His father was a deacon and a town official, and his grandfather a priest, but Patrick himself tells us that in his youth he did not take the faith seriously. At sixteen he was captured by Irish raiders and taken as a slave to Ireland, where he spent six years tending flocks in the mountains, suffering hunger and cold. It was there, in solitude, that he discovered God: he would pray a hundred times during the day and as many at night.

Escape and calling

One day he heard in a dream a voice saying that a ship was ready to take him home. He fled, walked many miles to the coast and managed to get on board. Back with his family, he had another dream: a man handed him letters headed "The voice of the Irish," and he heard the people of Ireland pleading: "We beg you, holy youth, to come and walk among us once more." Patrick understood that God was calling him to return as a missionary to the land where he had been a slave. He prepared, studied and was ordained a priest.

Apostle of Ireland

Around 432, now a bishop, he returned to Ireland. For about thirty years he traveled the island, preaching, baptizing thousands, ordaining priests and founding churches and communities. He faced the opposition of pagan chiefs and priests, was imprisoned several times and was in danger of death. Tradition says he used the shamrock, a small three-leafed plant, to explain the mystery of the Holy Trinity. He wrote the "Confession," in which he humbly recounts his life, and a courageous letter against a chieftain who had killed and enslaved newly baptized Christians.

"Christ with me"

A beautiful prayer known as "Saint Patrick's Breastplate" is attributed to him, which says: "Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ in me." He died on March 17, around the year 461. He is the patron of Ireland, and his day, March 17, is celebrated by Irish people all over the world.
cirilo-jerusalem:
Catechist of the Holy City

Cyril was born around the year 315 in or near Jerusalem, a few years after Emperor Constantine granted freedom to Christians. He received a good formation in the Scriptures and was ordained a priest. The bishop entrusted him with a very important task: preparing the catechumens, the adults who would receive Baptism on Easter night. Around the year 348, in the great Basilica of the Holy Sepulchre, built over the place of Jesus' death and resurrection, Cyril preached a series of catecheses that were written down and have come down to us.

The Catecheses

In these sermons Cyril explains the Creed phrase by phrase, simply and profoundly, and after Baptism he explains to the newly baptized the meaning of the sacraments they had received. He speaks with great faith of Christ's presence in the Eucharist and teaches how to receive it with reverence: "When you approach, make your left hand a throne for your right, which is to receive the King." These catecheses are still a treasure for understanding how the first Christians lived the faith and the liturgy.

Bishop and three times exiled

Around 350 Cyril became bishop of Jerusalem. Soon after, in 351, a great luminous cross appeared in the sky over the city, and he wrote to the emperor reporting the event. His time as bishop was marked by many struggles: a neighboring bishop who favored the Arians accused him unjustly, even of having sold church objects, when in fact he had sold them to feed the poor during a famine. Cyril was driven from his diocese three times, spending about sixteen years in exile.

Doctor of the Church

In 378 he was able to return to Jerusalem for good, and in 381 he took part in the Council of Constantinople, which confirmed the faith of Nicaea and completed the Creed we still pray today. He died in 386. In 1883 Pope Leo XIII declared him a Doctor of the Church. His memorial is celebrated on March 18.
turibio-mogrovejo:
A Spanish jurist

Turibius Alfonso de Mogrovejo was born on November 16, 1538, in Mayorga, Spain. He studied law at the universities of Valladolid, Salamanca and Coimbra, in Portugal, and became a professor. He was known for his intelligence, uprightness and life of prayer. King Philip II appointed him judge of an important tribunal in Granada, a post he held with justice, although he was a layman with no plans to become a priest.

From layman to archbishop

In 1579, to everyone's surprise, the king nominated him to be archbishop of Lima, Peru, a huge and difficult diocese in the New World. Turibius protested that he was not even a priest, but in the end he accepted it as God's will. He received holy orders, was ordained a priest and then a bishop in 1580, and arrived in Lima in 1581. His diocese stretched over thousands of kilometers of deserts, Andean mountains and forests.

The shepherd who crossed the Andes

Turibius learned Quechua and other indigenous languages so he could preach to and hear the confessions of the people directly. He visited the entire diocese three times, often on foot or by mule, facing cold, hunger and danger, over a total of thousands of kilometers. According to the accounts, he confirmed hundreds of thousands of people, among them Saint Rose of Lima. He firmly defended the indigenous people against the abuses of the Spanish colonizers, including powerful officials, which made him many enemies.

Organizer of the Church in America

In 1582 he convened the Third Council of Lima, which prepared a catechism in Spanish, Quechua and Aymara, one of the first books printed in South America. In 1591 he founded in Lima one of the first seminaries on the continent, as well as churches and hospitals. He died during a pastoral visit, in Saña, on Holy Thursday, March 23, 1606. He was canonized in 1726 and is the patron of the bishops of Latin America. His memorial is celebrated on March 23.
francisco-paula:
A child asked of Saint Francis

Francis was born on March 27, 1416, in Paola, in Calabria, southern Italy. His devout parents went for years without being able to have children and asked Saint Francis of Assisi for the grace, promising to give the boy the saint's name. When their son was born, they kept the promise. At thirteen Francis spent a year in a Franciscan friary, where he impressed the friars with his prayer and obedience. Afterward he made a pilgrimage with his parents to Assisi and Rome.

The hermit who founded the Minims

At fifteen he decided to live as a hermit in a cave near Paola, devoted to prayer and penance. Soon other young men wished to live as he did, and so a new religious community was born, which later received the name Order of Minims, meaning "the least of all," because of its humility. Besides the vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, the Minims took a vow to live always as in Lent, eating no meat, eggs or dairy. Francis's motto was a single word: "Charity."

Wonder-worker and friend of the poor

Many miracles were attributed to his prayers, and both the poor and the rich sought him out. It is said that in 1464, when a boatman refused to take him free of charge across the Strait of Messina, between Italy and Sicily, Francis spread his cloak on the water and crossed the sea with his companions. For this he is the patron of seafarers. He defended the poor before the powerful and was not afraid to correct unjust kings and nobles.

Counselor of kings

In 1483 King Louis XI of France, gravely ill, asked the Pope to send Francis to heal him. He went out of obedience to the Pope. He did not heal the king, but he helped him prepare to die at peace with God. He remained in France for twenty-five years, advising the following kings and founding friaries. He died on Good Friday, April 2, 1507, at ninety-one, and was canonized in 1519. His memorial is celebrated on April 2.
isidoro-sevilha:
A family of saints

Isidore was born around the year 560, probably in Cartagena, Spain, into a noble family that later moved to Seville. Three of his siblings are also venerated as saints: Leander and Fulgentius, who were bishops, and Florentina, who was an abbess. Since his parents died early, Isidore was educated by his older brother Leander, bishop of Seville, who was very demanding in his studies. A tradition says that, discouraged, the boy ran away from home, but on seeing how drops of water had worn a hole in a stone beside a well, he understood that perseverance overcomes all things and went back to his studies.

Bishop of Seville

At that time Spain was ruled by the Visigoths, who followed Arianism, a heresy that denied the divinity of Christ. Leander helped bring about the conversion of King Reccared and his people to the Catholic faith in 589. Around the year 600 Isidore succeeded his brother as bishop of Seville and governed the diocese for about thirty-six years. He presided over important councils, such as the Fourth Council of Toledo in 633, which called for schools for the formation of clergy beside the cathedrals. He also cared for the liturgy proper to Spain at that time.

The man who wanted to preserve all knowledge

Isidore was the most learned man of his time. His most famous work, the "Etymologies," is a great encyclopedia in twenty books that gathers the knowledge of the age: theology, grammar, history, medicine, geography, natural sciences and much more. Throughout the Middle Ages it was one of the most copied and studied books in Europe. He also wrote a history of the Goths and various works on the Bible and Christian life.

Doctor of the Church

Old and ill, he asked public forgiveness for his faults, distributed his goods to the poor and died in Seville on April 4, 636. In 1722 he was declared a Doctor of the Church. Because he gathered and organized so much knowledge, many remember him as a possible patron of the internet, although this is not official. His memorial is celebrated on April 4.
vicente-ferrer:
A Dominican from Valencia

Vincent Ferrer was born on January 23, 1350, in Valencia, Spain. At seventeen he entered the Order of Preachers, the Dominicans. He studied philosophy and theology in Barcelona, Lleida and Toulouse and soon became a well-known teacher and preacher. He was a man of intense prayer, fasting and great charity, and the example of his life made his words even more powerful.

Amid the Great Schism

Vincent lived in one of the saddest periods in the history of the Church, the Great Western Schism, when there were at the same time two and later even three men claiming to be Pope, one in Rome and another in Avignon, France. Christians were divided, and even holy people supported different sides. Vincent, in good faith, supported the Avignon Pope, Pedro de Luna, whose confessor he was. In 1398, gravely ill, he had a vision of Christ accompanied by Saint Dominic and Saint Francis, sending him to preach conversion throughout the world. He was healed and set out.

The preacher of Europe

For twenty years Vincent traveled on foot and by donkey through Spain, France, Italy and Switzerland, preaching in the open air to immense crowds, sometimes of thousands. He spoke of God's love, of repentance and of the Last Judgment, and many sinners were converted, enemies were reconciled and whole towns changed their ways. Many miracles were attributed to him. It is said that he preached in his own language, Valencian, and yet people of other languages understood him.

Working for unity

In time Vincent realized that Pedro de Luna refused to resign in order to end the division. In 1416 he withdrew his support, and this did much to end the schism, with the election of a single Pope, Martin V, in 1417. Vincent died in Vannes, in Brittany, France, on April 5, 1419. He was canonized in 1455. His memorial is celebrated on April 5.
joao-batista-lasalle:
A wealthy young man from Reims

John Baptist de La Salle was born on April 30, 1651, in Reims, France, the eldest child of a wealthy noble family. He felt the call to the priesthood very early, and at sixteen he was already a canon of Reims cathedral, a prestigious position. He studied in Paris, but when he was about twenty his parents died and he had to return home to care for his younger siblings. Even so, he continued his studies, was ordained a priest in 1678 and earned a doctorate in theology.

Meeting the poor schoolmasters

In 1679 he met Adrien Nyel, a layman who wanted to open free schools for the poor boys of Reims. John Baptist began to help him, without imagining where it would lead. Seeing that the teachers were poorly trained and discouraged, he took them to live in his own house to form them, which scandalized his family and society. Little by little he understood that God was calling him to devote his whole life to the education of the poor. In 1683 he gave up his canonry and, during a great famine, distributed his entire fortune to those in need.

The Brothers of the Christian Schools

With the teachers he founded the Brothers of the Christian Schools, religious laymen entirely devoted to teaching. Their schools brought many innovations: pupils were taught in classes rather than one by one; lessons were in French rather than Latin; teaching was free for the poor. He also created schools to train teachers, Sunday schools for young workers and technical courses. He faced lawsuits, the opposition of schoolmasters who felt threatened and even misunderstanding within the Church, but he never gave up.

Patron of teachers

He died on Good Friday, April 7, 1719, in Rouen, saying: "I adore in all things the will of God in my regard." He was canonized in 1900, and in 1950 Pope Pius XII declared him patron of teachers. Today Lasallian schools are found in dozens of countries. His memorial is celebrated on April 7.
estanislau:
The bishop of Kraków

Stanislaus was born on July 26, 1030, in Szczepanów, Poland, into a noble Christian family. According to tradition, his parents had him after many years of prayer. He studied for the priesthood and, after ordination, became a canon of Kraków cathedral, where he stood out as a preacher and for his charity to the poor. In 1072 he was chosen bishop of Kraków, then the capital of Poland. He visited the parishes, cared for the poor and firmly corrected abuses, making no distinction between rich and poor.

Before the king

King Bolesław II, called the Bold, was a great warrior but became cruel and lived a scandalous life. Stanislaus warned him several times, first privately and then publicly, to convert and stop oppressing the people. An ancient tradition says that, to discredit the bishop, he was accused of unjustly taking a piece of land; Stanislaus, in prayer, is said to have called as witness the former owner, already dead, who confirmed the sale before the court. Since the king did not change his ways, the bishop excommunicated him.

Martyred at the altar

Furious, Bolesław ordered his soldiers to kill the bishop, but they did not dare. So the king himself entered the small church of Saint Michael on Skałka hill in Kraków while Stanislaus was celebrating Mass and killed him with his sword on April 11, 1079. The body was cut into pieces, but the faithful gathered and venerated it. The bishop's death provoked a revolt, and the king had to flee the country, dying in exile.

Patron of Poland

Stanislaus was canonized in 1253 in Assisi. His relics are in Wawel Cathedral in Kraków, and he is one of the patrons of Poland. Saint John Paul II, who before becoming Pope was archbishop of Kraków, called him the patron of the moral order, because he defended to the end that not even kings are above the law of God. His memorial is celebrated on April 11.
anselmo:
A young man from the Alps

Anselm was born around 1033 in Aosta, a city at the foot of the Alps in northern Italy. His very devout mother taught him early to love God, and at fifteen he wanted to enter a monastery, but his father, a harsh man, would not allow it. After his mother's death Anselm drifted from the faith for a time and, because of conflicts with his father, left home. He spent some years traveling through France until he reached the abbey of Bec in Normandy, drawn by the reputation of the great teacher Lanfranc.

Monk, abbot and thinker

At Bec Anselm rediscovered his faith and became a monk in 1060. Because of his goodness and wisdom he was elected prior and later abbot. He was a loving father to the monks and a brilliant teacher. He wrote important works about God, such as the "Proslogion," in which he prays: "I do not seek to understand in order to believe, but I believe in order to understand." For him faith is not afraid of reason: it is a faith that seeks to understand ever more what it believes. He also wrote "Why God Became Man," explaining the mystery of the Incarnation and Redemption. For this he is called the father of scholastic theology.

Archbishop of Canterbury

In 1093 he was chosen archbishop of Canterbury, in England, almost by force. As archbishop he courageously defended the freedom of the Church against Kings William II and Henry I, who wanted to control the appointment of bishops and the property of the Church. For this he was exiled twice. At a council in London in 1102 he obtained the condemnation of the custom of selling people as if they were animals.

Doctor of the Church

Even in the midst of these struggles, Anselm kept praying, writing and caring for his people with gentleness. He died in Canterbury on April 21, 1109. In 1720 he was declared a Doctor of the Church. His memorial is celebrated on April 21.
fidelis-sigmaringen:
The lawyer of the poor

Mark Roy was born in 1578 in Sigmaringen, Germany. He studied philosophy and law at the University of Freiburg and earned a doctorate. For six years he accompanied young noblemen on study trips through Europe, being an example of prayer and Christian life for them. Then he began working as a lawyer in Alsace and became known as the "lawyer of the poor," because he defended free of charge those who could not pay. But he soon grew disillusioned with the injustice and corruption he saw in the courts.

Brother Fidelis

In 1612 he joined the Capuchin friars and received the name Fidelis, inspired by the words of Revelation: "Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life." He gave his goods to the poor and to needy students. Ordained a priest, he became a much sought-after preacher and superior of several friaries. When an epidemic struck the soldiers of an army, he cared for the sick with great dedication, without fear of contagion.

Missionary in Switzerland

At that time Europe was divided by wars and conflicts between Catholics and Protestants, mixed with political interests. In 1622 Fidelis was sent by the newly founded Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith to preach in the Grisons region of Switzerland. He preached with gentleness and firmness, visited families and spoke with everyone, and many people returned to the Catholic faith. Knowing that he was in danger, he prepared himself for martyrdom with prayer.

Faithful unto death

On April 24, 1622, after preaching in the church at Seewis, he was surrounded by a group of armed men who demanded that he renounce his faith. He refused and was killed with swords, praying and forgiving his attackers. He was the first martyr of the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith. Canonized in 1746, he is remembered as an example of fidelity to Christ and missionary courage. His memorial is celebrated on April 24.
marcos-evangelista:
John Mark of Jerusalem

Mark, also called John Mark, was the son of a woman named Mary, in whose house in Jerusalem the first Christians gathered to pray. It was there that Saint Peter went when an angel freed him from prison. Mark was a cousin of Barnabas, one of the great missionaries of the early Church. Many scholars think that the young man who ran away naked when Jesus was arrested in Gethsemane, an episode found only in Mark's Gospel, may be the evangelist himself.

Companion of Paul and Barnabas

Mark accompanied Paul and Barnabas on their first missionary journey, but partway through he left them and returned to Jerusalem. For this reason, when they set out on the second journey, Paul did not want to take him, and he and Barnabas ended up parting ways: Barnabas went on with Mark to Cyprus. In time, however, Mark matured and was reconciled with Paul, who, imprisoned in Rome, wrote to Timothy: "Bring Mark with you, for he is very useful to me in the ministry." It is a beautiful example that a failure is not the end of the story.

Peter's interpreter

Mark was also very close to Saint Peter, who affectionately calls him "my son Mark." Very ancient Christian writers relate that he was Peter's interpreter and faithfully set down in writing what the apostle preached about Jesus. So the Gospel of Mark was born, the shortest of the four and probably the first to be written, in Rome. It begins: "The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." It is a lively text, full of details, that shows Jesus in action.

The lion of Venice

According to tradition, Mark founded the Church of Alexandria, in Egypt, and died a martyr there. In the year 828 merchants from Venice carried his relics to their city, where the famous Basilica of Saint Mark was built in his honor. His symbol is the lion, because his Gospel begins with the voice of John the Baptist crying out in the wilderness. His feast is April 25.
jose-operario:
The carpenter of Nazareth

The Gospels tell us that Saint Joseph, the husband of the Virgin Mary, was a carpenter. The word used in the original Greek indicates a craftsman who worked with wood and perhaps also with stone, building doors, furniture, tools and parts of houses. It was hard and humble work, done with the hands, which provided for the Holy Family. Joseph was neither rich nor famous; he was an honest worker in a small village in Galilee.

Jesus, the carpenter's son

When Jesus began to preach, the people of Nazareth were amazed and asked: "Is this not the carpenter's son?" The Gospel of Mark even calls Jesus himself "the carpenter." This means that the Son of God spent most of his life on earth working, learning the trade from Joseph in the workshop at Nazareth. In this way Jesus gave human work an enormous dignity: work is not a punishment but a way of cooperating with God in creation, of serving others and of becoming holy.

A feast for workers

From the end of the nineteenth century the Popes began speaking a great deal about the rights of workers, who were often exploited in factories, with unjust wages and very long hours. Pope Leo XIII wrote about this in 1891 in the encyclical "Rerum Novarum." In 1955 Pope Pius XII established the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker on May 1, the day many countries celebrate Labor Day, to recall that work must serve the person, and the person must not be a slave to work.

Patron of all who work

Saint Joseph is a model for everyone who works: for those who have jobs and those looking for one, for those who work at home, in the fields, in cities and in factories. He teaches us to work honestly, with love for our families and offering everything to God. Pope Francis called him a "working father" and asked his intercession for all the unemployed. His memorial is celebrated on May 1.
atanasio:
A young deacon at Nicaea

Athanasius was born around the year 296 in Alexandria, Egypt, one of the largest cities of the Roman Empire. As a boy he lived through the effects of the last great persecution of Christians. He became a deacon and secretary to Bishop Alexander. At that time a priest named Arius was teaching that Jesus was not God like the Father but only the highest of creatures. In 325 Athanasius accompanied his bishop to the Council of Nicaea, which condemned this doctrine and proclaimed that the Son is "of the same substance as the Father," true God from true God, as we pray in the Creed.

Bishop of Alexandria

In 328, at just over thirty, Athanasius became bishop of Alexandria, an office he held for forty-five years. But Arianism did not disappear: many bishops and even emperors came to support it. Athanasius, however, defended the faith of Nicaea without yielding, even when he seemed to stand alone. From this came the famous expression "Athanasius against the world."

Five times exiled

Because of his firmness he was driven from his diocese five times by four different emperors, spending about seventeen years in exile in all. He was in Gaul, in Rome and, for years, hidden among the monks of the Egyptian desert, who protected and loved him. There he came to know Saint Anthony and wrote his biography, which spread the ideal of monastic life throughout the world. He also wrote "On the Incarnation of the Word," explaining that the Son of God became man so that we might share in the divine life.

Doctor of the Church

In 367, in an Easter letter, Athanasius listed the twenty-seven books of the New Testament exactly as we have them today, the first to do so. He spent his last years in peace in Alexandria and died on May 2, 373. He is one of the great Doctors of the Church of the East. His memorial is celebrated on May 2.
filipe-tiago:
Philip, the apostle who led others to Jesus

Philip was from Bethsaida in Galilee, the same town as Andrew and Peter. Jesus found him and said simply: "Follow me." Philip at once went to find his friend Nathanael and told him: "We have found him of whom Moses and the prophets wrote: Jesus of Nazareth." When Nathanael doubted, Philip replied: "Come and see." Later some Greeks who wanted to meet Jesus went precisely to Philip and asked him: "Sir, we wish to see Jesus."

"Show us the Father"

Before the multiplication of the loaves, Jesus asked Philip where they could buy bread for so many people, and he answered, worried, that not even two hundred silver coins would be enough. At the Last Supper Philip asked: "Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us." Jesus answered: "Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." According to tradition, after Pentecost Philip preached in Asia Minor and died a martyr in Hierapolis, in today's Turkey, where in 2011 archaeologists found what is believed to be his tomb.

James, servant of the Church in Jerusalem

James, son of Alphaeus, is called James the Less to distinguish him from the other apostle James, brother of John. The tradition of the Church in the West identifies him with James called "the brother of the Lord," that is, a relative of Jesus, who became the great leader of the Church in Jerusalem. He played an important role at the Council of Jerusalem, which decided that converted Gentiles did not need to follow all the Jewish laws. The Letter of James is attributed to him; it teaches that "faith without works is dead" and speaks of the anointing of the sick.

A shared feast

James was greatly respected for his prayer and uprightness, and he was martyred in Jerusalem around the year 62. The relics of the two apostles were taken to Rome and placed together in the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles in the sixth century. For this reason Philip and James are celebrated on the same day, May 3.
matias-apostolo:
An empty place among the Twelve

After the betrayal and death of Judas Iscariot, the group of the Twelve Apostles, whom Jesus had chosen as a sign of the twelve tribes of the new people of God, was incomplete. In the days between Jesus' Ascension and Pentecost, about a hundred and twenty disciples were gathered in prayer in Jerusalem, together with Mary, the mother of Jesus. Peter stood up and explained that someone had to be chosen to take Judas's place.

Witness of the Resurrection

Peter said that the one chosen should be one of the men who had accompanied Jesus throughout his ministry, from the baptism of John until the day he was taken up into heaven, so as to be, together with the apostles, a witness of his Resurrection. Two names were put forward: Joseph, called Barsabbas, and Matthias. This shows that Matthias had faithfully followed Jesus from the beginning, even without being part of the Twelve. Ancient Christian writers say he was one of the seventy-two disciples Jesus sent out on mission.

Chosen by God

The disciples prayed: "Lord, you who know the hearts of all, show us which of these two you have chosen." Then they cast lots, as was the custom among the Jews for discerning God's will, and the lot fell on Matthias, who was added to the apostles. A few days later he received the Holy Spirit with the others on the day of Pentecost. The Bible does not mention him again, which reminds us that what matters is not being famous but being faithful to the mission God entrusts to us.

Mission and martyrdom

The ancient traditions about Matthias's life differ: some say he preached in Judea, others in Cappadocia or by the Caspian Sea, and that he died a martyr. According to tradition, Saint Helena, mother of Emperor Constantine, brought part of his relics to Trier, in Germany, where they are still venerated today in an abbey bearing his name. His feast is celebrated on May 14.
isidro-lavrador:
A farm worker from Madrid

Isidore was born around the year 1080 in Madrid, Spain, which at that time was only a small town. His parents were poor and devout Christians and named him after Saint Isidore of Seville. Isidore never went to school, but at home he learned to pray and to love God. For almost his whole life he worked as a farmhand, tending the land of a wealthy landowner named Juan de Vargas on the outskirts of Madrid.

Husband and father

Isidore married María Toribia, a simple and devout young woman who is also venerated by the Church under the name Saint María de la Cabeza. The couple had a son. Tradition says that one day the boy fell into a deep well, and Isidore and María prayed with great faith; the water rose to the brim and brought the child up alive. The two lived simply, prayed together and shared the little they had with those who had even less.

The angels who plowed the land

Every morning Isidore went to Mass before starting work in the fields. Some jealous fellow workers complained to their employer that he arrived late and worked less. Juan de Vargas went to see and, according to tradition, saw two angels with white oxen plowing beside Isidore, so that his work produced more than that of the others. Other miracles are also told: in a harsh winter Isidore gave part of his seed to hungry birds, and yet the sack remained full; and the pot in his house was never empty for the poor who knocked at the door.

Patron of farmers

Isidore died on May 15, 1130, in Madrid. Forty years later his body was found incorrupt. He was canonized in 1622, on the same day as Saint Ignatius of Loyola, Saint Francis Xavier, Saint Teresa of Ávila and Saint Philip Neri. He is the patron of Madrid and of farmers and rural workers, and he shows that it is possible to become a saint in everyday work. His memorial is celebrated on May 15.
bernardino-sena:
The young man who nursed plague victims

Bernardine was born on September 8, 1380, in Massa Marittima, in Tuscany, Italy, into a noble family. He lost his mother at three and his father at six, and was raised by very devout aunts in Siena. He was a cheerful, studious and much loved young man. In 1400, when plague struck Siena and many were fleeing the city, Bernardine, about twenty years old, took charge with a group of friends of the city's great hospital for four months, tending the sick day and night and burying the dead.

Friar and preacher

In 1402 he joined the Franciscan friars, in the Observant branch, which sought to live Saint Francis's poverty more strictly. He was ordained a priest and, after some years of prayer and study, began to preach. He became the greatest popular preacher in the Italy of his time. He traveled the cities on foot and preached in the squares, sometimes for hours, to immense crowds, in simple language, with everyday examples and plenty of good humor. He fought against usury, gambling, vanities and above all the rivalries and hatreds between families and parties that divided the cities.

The Holy Name of Jesus

Bernardine spread devotion to the Holy Name of Jesus. He had the letters IHS, the first letters of the name of Jesus in Greek, painted on a tablet, surrounded by golden rays of sunlight on a blue background, and invited the people to venerate the name of the Lord. Many cities began placing this symbol over the doors of houses and public buildings, in place of the coats of arms of the factions. Some accused him of promoting superstition, but Pope Martin V examined the case and declared him innocent.

Humble to the end

Bernardine refused three times to become a bishop, preferring to remain a simple preacher. As vicar general of his Franciscan family, he helped it grow greatly. He died on May 20, 1444, in L'Aquila, during a preaching journey, and was canonized only six years later. His memorial is celebrated on May 20.
beda-veneravel:
A boy entrusted to the monastery

Bede was born around the year 673 in the north of England, in the region of Northumbria. At seven his family entrusted him to the monks of the monastery of Saint Peter at Wearmouth, and later he moved to the sister monastery of Saint Paul at Jarrow, where he lived the rest of his life. While he was still a boy, an epidemic killed almost all the monks of Jarrow. It is said that only the abbot and a boy, probably Bede himself, survived, and that the two kept singing the monastery's prayers alone until new monks arrived.

Learning, teaching and writing

Bede was ordained a deacon at nineteen and a priest at thirty. He never left his region, but the monastery library, one of the best in Europe, opened the whole world to him. He wrote: "I devoted myself entirely to the study of the Scriptures, and amid the observance of the rule and the daily singing in church, I always took delight in learning, teaching and writing." He wrote about forty works: commentaries on the Bible, lives of saints, poetry and scientific treatises, such as one on the reckoning of time and the date of Easter.

Father of English history

His most famous work is the "Ecclesiastical History of the English People," completed in 731, which tells how the faith reached and spread through England. Bede researched carefully, consulted documents and witnesses and named his sources, something rare at the time. For this he is called the father of English history. It was also thanks to him that the custom spread of counting the years from the birth of Christ, as we still do today.

A peaceful death

On the eve of the Ascension in the year 735, already very ill, Bede was dictating a translation of the Gospel of John into the language of the people. The young man writing told him: "Only one sentence is left." Bede dictated it and replied: "It is finished." He asked to be laid on the floor of his cell, facing the place where he used to pray, sang the "Glory Be" and died on May 26, 735. Soon afterward he was already being called "Venerable." In 1899 he was declared a Doctor of the Church. His memorial is celebrated on May 25.
filipe-neri:
"Good little Pippo" of Florence

Philip Neri was born on July 21, 1515, in Florence, Italy. He was such a cheerful and obedient boy that people called him "Pippo buono," "good little Phil." At eighteen he was sent to work with an uncle who was a merchant and thought of making him his heir. But Philip felt that God was calling him to something else. He left everything and went to Rome without money, where he lodged in the house of a Florentine, teaching his sons in exchange for a room and a little food.

Apostle of the streets of Rome

For seventeen years, still a layman, Philip went through the streets, squares and shops of Rome talking with all kinds of people, especially the young, and inviting them to change their lives, with good humor and affection. He used to ask: "Well, brothers, when shall we begin to do good?" At night he prayed alone in the catacombs. In 1544, on the feast of Pentecost, while he was praying, he felt a ball of fire enter his chest, and from then on his heart pounded whenever he prayed. He founded a confraternity to welcome poor pilgrims and the sick who were leaving the hospitals.

The Oratory

In 1551, at thirty-six, he was ordained a priest. He spent hours in the confessional, and in the afternoons he gathered people of every class in his room to read the Bible, pray, talk about the lives of the saints and sing. These gatherings were called the "Oratory," and the music composed for them gave rise to the musical form called the oratorio. He also organized pilgrimages on foot to the seven main churches of Rome, with picnics and singing. From this group the Congregation of the Oratory was born, approved in 1575.

The saint of joy

Philip was very humble, and to avoid being admired he sometimes did funny things in public. He said that a cheerful heart reaches perfection more easily than a sad one, and he joked: "Scruples and melancholy, out of my house!" Popes, cardinals and simple people sought him out for advice. He died on May 26, 1595, and was canonized in 1622. He is called the "apostle of Rome" and the "saint of joy." His memorial is celebrated on May 26.
justino-martir:
A philosopher seeking the truth

Justin was born around the year 100 in Flavia Neapolis, in Samaria, today's Nablus, into a pagan family of Greek origin. From his youth he wanted to know the truth about God and the meaning of life. So he sought out several teachers of philosophy: a Stoic who could not tell him about God; another who immediately asked him for money; a third who demanded that he first learn music, geometry and astronomy. Finally he grew enthusiastic about the philosophy of Plato, thinking he was close to seeing God.

Meeting an old man

One day, walking alone near the sea to meditate, he met an elderly man who spoke with him at length. The old man told him about the prophets of Israel, who had announced the coming of Christ, and invited him to pray that the gates of light might be opened to him. Justin says that at that moment "a fire was kindled" in his soul, and he came to love the prophets and the friends of Christ. He was converted and baptized around the year 130.

Defender of the faith

Justin kept wearing the philosopher's cloak and opened a school in Rome, where he taught that Christianity is the true philosophy. He wrote two "Apologies," that is, defenses of the Christians, addressed to the emperors, showing that Christians were not criminals but good citizens. He taught that among all peoples there were "seeds of the Word," small lights of truth that prepared them for Christ. In one of these works he left the oldest description of Sunday Mass: the reading of the writings of the apostles and prophets, the homily, the prayers, the consecrated bread and wine and the collection for the poor. It is moving to see that today's Mass is the same as then.

The martyrdom

Justin was denounced by a rival philosopher and arrested with six companions. Before the prefect of Rome, Rusticus, he firmly declared his faith and refused to offer sacrifice to the gods. The records of the trial have come down to us. He was beheaded around the year 165. He is the patron of philosophers. His memorial is celebrated on June 1.
carlos-lwanga:
The faith reaches Uganda

At the end of the nineteenth century, Anglican and Catholic missionaries arrived in the kingdom of Buganda, in today's Uganda, in the heart of Africa. The Catholic missionaries were the Missionaries of Africa, known as the White Fathers, who arrived in 1879. Many young people, especially the pages who served at the king's court, became interested in the faith, learned the catechism and asked for Baptism. In Christ they found a freedom and dignity they had not known.

King Mwanga

In 1884 Mwanga II became king. At first he seemed favorable to the Christians, but he soon came to see them as a threat to his absolute power, especially because the Christian pages refused his immoral advances. Joseph Mukasa, head of the pages and a Catholic, rebuked the king for having an Anglican bishop killed and protected the young men. For this he was beheaded in November 1885, becoming the first martyr. That same night Charles Lwanga, who took his place as head of the pages, was baptized.

Protector of the young

Charles Lwanga, then just over twenty, kept protecting the pages and teaching them the faith. In May 1886 the king discovered that the young men were still praying and ordered the Christians to come forward. The night before, Charles had secretly baptized some catechumens, among them little Kizito, only fourteen. Before the king the young men stepped forward and declared that they were Christians and would remain faithful until death.

The fires of Namugongo

The prisoners were marched on foot to Namugongo, and on June 3, 1886, Ascension Day, they were burned alive. Charles was burned separately, slowly. He said to the executioner: "It is as if you were pouring water on me. I beg you to repent and become a Christian like me." His last words were: "My God!" Together with Catholics, young Anglicans also died for the faith. The twenty-two Catholic martyrs were canonized in 1964 by Paul VI. Every June 3, millions of pilgrims go to Namugongo. Charles Lwanga is the patron of African youth. His memorial is June 3.
bonifacio:
The English monk Winfrid

Boniface, whose baptismal name was Winfrid, was born around the year 675 in the kingdom of Wessex, England. As a child, listening to monks who visited his home, he wanted to follow the religious life and was educated in monasteries. He became a monk and a highly esteemed teacher and wrote a Latin grammar. But he felt a strong desire to bring the Gospel to the Germanic peoples of the continent, who were kin to the English and still lived in paganism. In 716 he made a first attempt in Frisia, in today's Netherlands, but war forced him to return.

Sent by the Pope

In 719 he went to Rome, and Pope Gregory II gave him the name Boniface and officially sent him as a missionary to Germany. He worked in Frisia, Hesse and Thuringia, and in 722 he was ordained a bishop. At Geismar the pagans venerated an enormous oak dedicated to the god Thor. Before a crowd Boniface had the tree cut down. Since no lightning struck him, many understood that those gods had no power and asked for Baptism. With the wood of the oak a chapel dedicated to Saint Peter was built.

Organizer of the Church in Germany

Appointed archbishop, Boniface founded dioceses such as Salzburg, Regensburg, Passau, Würzburg and Eichstätt, and several monasteries, among them Fulda, which became a great center of faith and culture. He called monks and nuns from England to help him, such as Saint Lioba. He convened councils to reform the Church among the Franks and always worked in deep union with the Pope. He became archbishop of Mainz.

Martyr in Frisia

Nearly eighty years old, he wanted to return to his first mission in Frisia. On June 5, 754, near Dokkum, while waiting for a group of newly baptized people to confirm them, he was attacked by an armed band. He forbade his companions to fight, saying that evil must not be repaid with evil, and shielded his head with a book of the Gospels. He was killed with more than fifty companions and buried at Fulda. He is called the "apostle of Germany." His memorial is June 5.
barnabe-apostolo:
The son of encouragement

Barnabas was named Joseph and was a Levite born on the island of Cyprus. The apostles gave him the nickname Barnabas, which means "son of consolation" or "son of encouragement," because he had the gift of encouraging and uniting people. The Acts of the Apostles tell that he sold a field he owned and gave all the money to the apostles to help the poor of the Jerusalem community. The Bible describes him as "a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith."

The friend who believed in Paul

When Saul, the former persecutor, was converted and went to Jerusalem, the disciples were afraid of him and did not believe he was truly a Christian. It was Barnabas who welcomed him, brought him to the apostles and told how he had met the Lord on the road to Damascus. Later, sent by the Church of Jerusalem to Antioch, Barnabas rejoiced to see so many conversions and went to Tarsus to bring Paul so they could work together. For a whole year they taught there, and it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called "Christians."

Missionary with Paul

One day, while the community of Antioch was praying, the Holy Spirit said: "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them." So began the first missionary journey, through Cyprus and Asia Minor. In Lystra, after a healing, the people thought Barnabas was the god Zeus and Paul the god Hermes, and the two had to stop them from offering sacrifices to them. Barnabas and Paul also defended, at the Council of Jerusalem, that Gentiles could be Christians without following the whole Jewish law.

A second chance for Mark

Before the second journey, Barnabas wanted to take his cousin John Mark again, who had left them during the first. Paul did not agree, and the two parted ways. Barnabas went with Mark to Cyprus, giving him a new opportunity, and Mark later became an evangelist. According to tradition, Barnabas died a martyr in Salamis, Cyprus. Although he was not one of the Twelve, he is called an apostle. His memorial is celebrated on June 11.
luis-gonzaga:
Heir to a marquis

Aloysius Gonzaga was born on March 9, 1568, in the castle of Castiglione delle Stiviere in northern Italy. He was the eldest son of Ferrante Gonzaga, a marquis from one of the most powerful families in Italy, and his father dreamed of making him a great soldier. At four he was already walking around the army camp in a small suit of armor. But at about seven Aloysius began to feel a great love for God and started to pray a great deal, with a seriousness rare in a child.

At court, but with his heart in God

While still a boy he was sent as a page to the Medici court in Florence and later to the court of King Philip II in Spain. Amid the luxury, parties and intrigues, Aloysius remained recollected and prayed. At nine, in Florence, he consecrated his purity to Our Lady. At twelve he received his First Communion from Saint Charles Borromeo. The desire grew in him to become a Jesuit, to serve God and souls.

The renunciation

When Aloysius told his father he wanted to become a religious, the marquis was furious and for years did everything to make him change his mind. But Aloysius stood firm, and at last his father gave in. In 1585, at seventeen, Aloysius renounced his title and inheritance in favor of his younger brother and entered the Jesuit novitiate in Rome. His spiritual director was Saint Robert Bellarmine. He said humbly that he was like a bent piece of iron that needed to be straightened.

Serving the plague-stricken

In 1591 a severe epidemic struck Rome. The Jesuits went to serve in the hospitals, and Aloysius asked to go as well. He washed and fed the sick, made their beds and prepared them for the sacraments. One day he found an abandoned sick man in the street, carried him on his back to the hospital and cared for him. He caught the disease and died on June 21, 1591, at only twenty-three, with his eyes on the crucifix and the name of Jesus on his lips. He was canonized in 1726 and is the patron of youth and students. His memorial is June 21.
tomas-more:
A young London lawyer

Thomas More was born on February 7, 1478, in London, the son of a judge. He studied at Oxford and then law in London, becoming a brilliant and honest lawyer. For some years he lived near the Carthusian monks, praying with them and thinking of becoming a religious, but he understood that God was calling him to marriage and public life. He married and had four children. After his first wife died, he married again. His home was joyful, full of books, music and prayer, and he made a point of giving his daughters the same education as his son, something rare at the time.

Writer and statesman

Thomas was a friend of the great scholars of his day, such as Erasmus of Rotterdam, and wrote the famous book "Utopia," about an imaginary, more just society. He entered politics, was a member and Speaker of Parliament and a diplomat, and in 1529 King Henry VIII appointed him Lord Chancellor, the highest office in the kingdom after the king. He was known for his justice, his refusal to accept gifts and his kindness to the poor. Despite his power, he kept praying every day and doing penance in secret.

Faithful to conscience

Henry VIII wanted to annul his marriage to Queen Catherine in order to marry Anne Boleyn. Since the Pope would not accept this, the king broke with Rome and declared himself head of the Church in England. Thomas could not accept this in conscience, and in 1532 he resigned as chancellor. In 1534 he refused to take the oath demanded by the king, which denied the Pope's authority, and was imprisoned in the Tower of London. He remained there fifteen months, praying and writing letters full of faith and tenderness to his daughter Margaret.

"The king's good servant, but God's first"

Condemned for treason on the basis of false testimony, he was beheaded on July 6, 1535. On the scaffold he declared that he died "the king's good servant, but God's first," and even joked with the executioner, showing his inner peace. He was canonized in 1935, together with Saint John Fisher, a bishop martyred for the same reason. In 2000 John Paul II proclaimed him patron of statesmen and politicians. His memorial is celebrated on June 22.
nascimento-joao-batista:
Zechariah and Elizabeth

The Gospel of Luke tells that in the days of King Herod there lived a priest named Zechariah, married to Elizabeth. Both were "righteous before God," but they had no children, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were already old. One day, while Zechariah was offering incense in the Temple in Jerusalem, the angel Gabriel appeared to him and announced: "Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall name him John. He will be great before the Lord, he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb, and he will make ready a people prepared for the Lord."

Zechariah's silence

Zechariah doubted: how could this be, since he and his wife were so old? So the angel told him he would be unable to speak until everything was fulfilled. Elizabeth conceived and said, full of joy, that the Lord had looked upon her. In the sixth month of her pregnancy she was visited by her kinswoman Mary, who was already carrying Jesus in her womb. As soon as she heard Mary's greeting, the child John leapt for joy within Elizabeth.

"His name is John"

When the child was born, the neighbors and relatives rejoiced with Elizabeth. On the eighth day they wanted to name him after his father, Zechariah, but Elizabeth said: "No, he shall be called John." They asked the father by signs, and he asked for a tablet and wrote: "His name is John." At that moment his mouth was opened and he began to praise God with the canticle "Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel," which the Church still prays every morning. And everyone wondered: "What then will this child be?"

A feast of light

The Church celebrates the birth of only three people: Jesus, Mary and John the Baptist, because John was sanctified even before he was born. The feast is on June 24, six months before Christmas. Saint Augustine observed that after this date the days begin to grow shorter in the northern part of the world, and after Christmas they begin to grow longer, recalling John's words: "He must increase, and I must decrease." In Brazil this feast is celebrated with bonfires, folk dances and traditional food at the June festivals.
ireneu-lyon:
The boy who heard Polycarp

Irenaeus was born around the year 130 in Smyrna, in Asia Minor, today's Turkey. As a boy he listened to the preaching of Bishop Saint Polycarp, who had known the apostle Saint John. In old age Irenaeus wrote that he remembered the place where Polycarp sat to teach and how he recounted what he had heard from John about the Lord. So Irenaeus received the faith from a source very close to the apostles.

Bishop of Lyon

Later Irenaeus went to Gaul, today's France, and became a priest in Lyon. In 177 the Christian community of Lyon suffered a terrible persecution in which many martyrs died, among them Bishop Pothinus, ninety years old, and the young slave Blandina. Irenaeus escaped because he was in Rome, carrying a letter from the community to the Pope. When he returned, he was chosen to succeed Pothinus as bishop of Lyon. He also preached the Gospel to the Celtic peoples of the region, learning their language.

Against the false teachers

At that time some groups called Gnostics claimed to have a secret knowledge reserved for a few, and taught that the material world was evil and that the God of the Old Testament was different from the Father of Jesus. Irenaeus wrote a great work, "Against Heresies," showing that the true faith is not secret: it is what the apostles preached publicly and what was handed on by the bishops, their successors, in all the Churches, especially that of Rome. He defended the goodness of creation and of the body and wrote: "The glory of God is man fully alive, and the life of man is the vision of God."

Doctor of Unity

Irenaeus also taught that Mary is the new Eve: "The knot of Eve's disobedience was untied by Mary's obedience," a phrase that inspired devotion to Our Lady Untier of Knots. His name means "peaceful," and he lived up to it by helping to settle, with charity, a dispute about the date of Easter. He died around the year 202. In 2022 Pope Francis declared him a Doctor of the Church with the title "Doctor of Unity." His memorial is June 28.
pedro-paulo-apostolos:
Peter, the fisherman who became rock

Simon was a fisherman from Galilee, the brother of Andrew. Jesus called him by the sea and said: "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men." Simon left his nets and followed him. Near Caesarea Philippi, when Jesus asked the disciples who they said he was, Simon answered: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Jesus then told him: "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church." Peter was impulsive and generous: he walked on the water and sank out of fear, promised never to abandon Jesus and denied him three times on the night of the Passion, but afterward wept bitterly.

"Feed my sheep"

After the Resurrection, by the lake, Jesus asked Peter three times: "Simon, do you love me?" And three times he entrusted to him: "Feed my sheep." On the day of Pentecost, filled with the Holy Spirit, Peter preached boldly, and about three thousand people were baptized. He guided the Church in Jerusalem, in Antioch and finally in Rome. There he died a martyr during Nero's persecution, crucified, according to tradition, upside down, because he did not consider himself worthy to die as the Lord had. His tomb lies beneath Saint Peter's Basilica in the Vatican.

Paul, the apostle to the nations

Paul, the former persecutor Saul, was transformed by his encounter with Christ on the road to Damascus. He traveled thousands of kilometers proclaiming the Gospel to the Gentiles, founded communities and wrote letters that still nourish the Church's faith today. At the end of his life, imprisoned in Rome, he wrote: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith." As a Roman citizen he was beheaded, also in Rome, outside the city walls, where the Basilica of Saint Paul stands today.

The two pillars of the Church

Peter and Paul were very different: a simple fisherman and a scholar of the Law; one called to guide the Church, the other sent to the ends of the earth. They even argued, yet they were united in their love for Christ and gave their lives for him in the same city. That is why the Church has celebrated them together since the first centuries, as the two pillars of the faith. On this day new archbishops receive the pallium from the Pope as a sign of communion, and in Brazil people also pray in a special way for the Pope. The solemnity is June 29.
junipero-serra:
A professor from Majorca

Miquel Josep Serra was born on November 24, 1713, in Petra, on the island of Majorca, Spain, into a farming family. At sixteen he joined the Franciscan friars and received the name Junípero, in honor of one of Saint Francis's companions. He became a brilliant professor of philosophy and theology and a much sought-after preacher. But at thirty-five he left his academic career to fulfill an old dream: to be a missionary in the New World.

Missionary in Mexico

In 1749 he arrived in Mexico. He insisted on walking to the capital, and on the way he suffered an injury to his leg that troubled him for the rest of his life. For eight years he worked with the Pame people in the Sierra Gorda, learning their language, teaching new farming techniques and building churches with them that are now World Heritage sites. Then he spent years preaching parish missions throughout Mexico.

The missions of California

In 1769, at fifty-five, he set out with an expedition to Alta California, a region that now belongs to the United States. On July 16 of that year he founded the mission of San Diego, the first of nine missions he founded himself, among them those that gave rise to cities such as San Francisco and San Juan Capistrano. Despite his bad leg he traveled thousands of kilometers, often on foot, baptizing, confirming and teaching. His motto was: "Always forward, never back." He defended the native peoples against abuses by Spanish soldiers and wrote to the viceroy asking for laws to protect them.

Saint of the Americas

He died on August 28, 1784, at the mission of Carmel, where he is buried. In 2015 Pope Francis canonized him in Washington, in the first canonization held on United States soil. On that occasion the Pope also acknowledged the sufferings of the indigenous peoples during colonization and recalled Junípero's efforts to defend them. His memorial is celebrated on July 1.
tome-apostolo:
The courageous apostle

Thomas, also called Didymus, which means "twin," was one of the Twelve Apostles. The Gospel of John reveals something of his character. When Jesus decided to return to Judea, where people wanted to stone him, in order to visit his friend Lazarus, the disciples were afraid, but Thomas said: "Let us also go, that we may die with him." He was a loyal, sincere and direct man who said what he thought.

"How can we know the way?"

At the Last Supper, when Jesus said he was going to prepare a place for the disciples and that they knew the way, Thomas frankly admitted: "Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?" Thomas's sincere question gave us one of Jesus' most beautiful sayings: "I am the Way, the Truth and the Life. No one comes to the Father except through me."

"My Lord and my God!"

On the Sunday of the Resurrection, Jesus appeared to the disciples, but Thomas was not with them. When they told him, he replied: "Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands and put my finger into his side, I will not believe." Eight days later Jesus appeared again and said to Thomas: "Put your finger here and see my hands; do not be unbelieving, but believe." Thomas then made the most beautiful profession of faith in the Gospels: "My Lord and my God!" And Jesus said: "Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed." Saint Gregory the Great remarked that Thomas's doubt was more useful to our faith than the faith of those who believed at once.

Apostle of India

According to an ancient tradition, after Pentecost Thomas preached in Persia and reached India, where he founded Christian communities. Even today in southern India there are Christians who call themselves "Saint Thomas Christians" and consider themselves his children in the faith. He is said to have died a martyr, pierced by a spear, near the present-day city of Chennai, where his tomb is venerated. He is the patron of India. His feast is celebrated on July 3.
henrique-imperador:
A duke educated by a saint

Henry was born on May 6, 973, in Bavaria, in today's Germany, the son of Duke Henry of Bavaria. His teacher was Saint Wolfgang, bishop of Regensburg, who taught him the faith, prayer and love for the Church. In 995, on his father's death, he became Duke of Bavaria. In 1002 he was elected King of Germany, and in 1014 he was crowned emperor in Rome by Pope Benedict VIII. He married Cunigunde of Luxembourg, who is also venerated as a saint.

A Christian ruler

Henry sought to govern according to the Gospel. He worked for peace among peoples, for justice and for the reform of the Church, which suffered from corruption and an ignorant clergy. He supported reformed monasteries and took care to choose worthy, well-prepared bishops. He was very generous to the poor and to the churches. As ruler of an enormous empire he had to face wars and revolts, but he always sought reconciliation.

The diocese of Bamberg

In 1007 Henry founded the diocese of Bamberg, which became a great center of faith and culture, and had a beautiful cathedral built there. A tradition says that one day he asked to enter a monastery in Verdun as a monk. The abbot accepted and told him that as a monk he owed obedience; then he ordered him to return to governing the empire, because that was where God wanted him to serve. Henry obeyed and continued to reign as a true servant of God and of the people.

Patron of Benedictine oblates

Henry and Cunigunde had no children. He died on July 13, 1024, and was buried in Bamberg Cathedral, where his wife was later buried as well. He was canonized in 1146 by Pope Eugene III. He is the patron of Benedictine oblates, lay people who live in the world following the spirit of Saint Benedict, and he shows that it is possible to be holy even in the highest offices and amid political responsibilities. His memorial is celebrated on July 13.
lourenco-brindes:
A Capuchin with a prodigious memory

Giulio Cesare Russo was born on July 22, 1559, in Brindisi, in southern Italy. His father died when he was still a child, and he was educated first by the Franciscan friars and then by an uncle in Venice. At sixteen he joined the Capuchin friars, receiving the name Lawrence. He studied in Padua and showed an extraordinary intelligence: he learned Hebrew, Greek, German, Spanish, French and other languages, and knew almost the whole Bible by heart in the original languages.

Preacher across Europe

Ordained a priest in 1582, he became a famous preacher throughout Italy. In 1599 the Pope sent him to Austria, Bohemia and Germany to found Capuchin friaries and strengthen the Catholic faith at a time of many divisions. He preached with clarity and charity, held dialogues with scholars and cared for the poor and the sick. He wrote many sermons, especially about Our Lady, to whom he had great devotion.

The friar at the head of the army

In 1601, when Turkish armies were threatening Europe, Lawrence was appointed chaplain to the Christian troops in Hungary. Before the battle of Székesfehérvár he encouraged the soldiers, who were far fewer than the enemy. During the fighting he rode at the head of the troops, unarmed, carrying only a crucifix in his hand. The Christians won, and many attributed the victory to his prayer and courage. In 1602 he was elected minister general of the Capuchins and visited the order's friaries in several countries on foot.

Apostolic Doctor

He was also entrusted with several diplomatic missions for peace among Catholic rulers. In 1619, already ill, he traveled to Lisbon to ask the King of Spain to protect the people of Naples from the abuses of a governor. There he died on July 22, 1619, the day he turned sixty. He was canonized in 1881, and in 1959 Pope John XXIII declared him a Doctor of the Church with the title "Apostolic Doctor." His memorial is July 21.
maria-madalena:
The woman of Magdala

Mary came from Magdala, a town on the shores of the Sea of Galilee, which is why she is called Mary Magdalene. The Gospels say that Jesus cast seven demons out of her, that is, he freed her from a very great evil. From then on, full of gratitude, she followed Jesus together with other women who accompanied the Master and the apostles and supported them with their means. Over the centuries in the West she was often confused with the sinful woman who anointed Jesus' feet and with Mary of Bethany, but the Gospels do not say they were the same person.

Faithful to the cross

When Jesus was arrested and crucified, almost all the disciples fled. Mary Magdalene, however, remained at the foot of the cross, together with Mary, the mother of Jesus, and the disciple John. She saw where the Lord's body was buried. Her love was stronger than fear, and she did not abandon Jesus even in the darkest hour.

"Mary!" "Teacher!"

On the first day of the week, very early, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene went to the tomb and found the stone rolled away. She ran to tell Peter and John. Then she stood outside, weeping. She saw a man she thought was the gardener and asked him to tell her where he had put Jesus' body. The man called her by name: "Mary!" She recognized him and cried out: "Rabboni!" which means "Teacher." Jesus told her: "Go and tell my brothers that I am ascending to my Father and your Father." She ran and announced to the disciples: "I have seen the Lord!"

Apostle to the apostles

Because she was the first witness of the Resurrection and the first to announce it to the apostles, the ancient Fathers of the Church called her the "apostle to the apostles." Later traditions say she ended her days in the south of France, in prayer. In 2016 Pope Francis raised her memorial to the rank of a feast, the same as the apostles, to highlight her mission. Her feast is celebrated on July 22.
brigida-suecia:
A noble girl from Sweden

Bridget was born in 1303 in Finsta, Sweden, into a noble and deeply Christian family related to the royal family. Her mother died when she was about twelve, and she was raised by an aunt. At ten she had a vision of Jesus crucified that marked her forever. She asked him who had wounded him so, and heard the answer: those who scorn his love. From then on the Passion of Christ held a central place in her prayer.

Wife and mother of eight

At thirteen she married Ulf Gudmarsson, a young nobleman. They were married for twenty-eight years and had eight children, among them Saint Catherine of Sweden. The couple lived their faith deeply, prayed together and helped the poor. Bridget also served at the court of King Magnus IV as counselor to the queen and was not afraid to warn the king when he acted wrongly. In 1341 she and her husband made a pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela. On the way back Ulf fell ill, and soon afterward he died in a Cistercian monastery.

Foundress and prophet

As a widow, Bridget devoted herself entirely to God. She received many revelations about the life of Christ and Mary and about the state of the Church, which were written down by her confessors. She founded the Order of the Most Holy Savior, known as the Bridgettines, with its main house in Vadstena, Sweden. In 1349 she went to Rome and stayed there for the rest of her life, praying, serving the poor and pilgrims and urging the Popes, who were then living in Avignon, France, to return to Rome.

Patroness of Europe

At almost seventy she made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land. She died in Rome on July 23, 1373, and was canonized in 1391. She is the patron saint of Sweden, and in 1999 Saint John Paul II proclaimed her co-patroness of Europe, together with Saint Catherine of Siena and Saint Teresa Benedicta of the Cross. Her feast is celebrated on July 23.
joaquim-ana:
The parents of Our Lady

The Bible does not give the names of the Virgin Mary's parents. What we know about them comes from a very ancient tradition, recorded mainly in a second-century writing called the Protoevangelium of James. This text is not part of the Bible, but it preserved memories that the Church has lovingly embraced, such as the names Joachim and Anne. Since the first centuries Christians have venerated them as the grandparents of Jesus.

The sorrow of having no children

According to this tradition, Joachim was a just and generous man who shared his goods with the Temple and the poor. He and Anne lived in Jerusalem and loved each other dearly, but they suffered because they had no children, which at that time was seen as a great misfortune. One day Joachim's offering was refused at the Temple precisely for this reason. Humiliated, he withdrew into the desert to pray and fast. Anne, at home, also wept and prayed, asking God to give her a child.

God's answer

Tradition says that an angel appeared to each of them, announcing that God had heard their prayers and that they would have a daughter who would be blessed by all generations. Joachim hurried back to Jerusalem, and the two met and embraced at the Golden Gate of the city, full of joy. So Mary was born, and Anne and Joachim raised her in the love of God and consecrated her to the Lord. In Jerusalem, near the Pool of Bethesda, there is an ancient church dedicated to Saint Anne on the spot where, according to tradition, the family's house stood.

Patrons of grandparents

Joachim and Anne remind us of the value of patience in prayer and of faith handed on in the family. As the grandparents of Jesus, they are the patrons of grandparents. In Brazil, July 26 is also Grandparents' Day, and in 2021 Pope Francis established the World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly, celebrated on the fourth Sunday of July, close to this feast. Their memorial is celebrated on July 26.
marta-maria-lazaro:
The friends of Bethany

In Bethany, a small village near Jerusalem, lived three siblings: Martha, Mary and Lazarus. The Gospel of John says something very beautiful about them: "Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus." Their house was a place where Jesus felt at home with family, where he could rest and be welcomed with affection, especially when he went up to Jerusalem. In 2021 Pope Francis decided that the three siblings would be celebrated together on the same day.

"Only one thing is needed"

Once, when Jesus was at their house, Martha was busy with many tasks to serve the guest well, while Mary sat at Jesus' feet listening to his word. Martha complained: "Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to do all the serving alone?" Jesus answered kindly: "Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but only one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the better part, and it will not be taken from her." Jesus did not despise Martha's service, but taught that everything must spring from listening to God.

"I am the resurrection and the life"

One day Lazarus fell gravely ill, and his sisters sent word to Jesus: "Lord, the one you love is ill." When Jesus arrived, Lazarus had already been dead for four days. Martha went out to meet him and said: "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died." Jesus replied: "I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live." And Martha made a beautiful profession of faith: "Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God." Before the tomb, Jesus wept. Then he cried out: "Lazarus, come out!" and Lazarus came out alive.

The perfume that filled the house

Six days before the Passover, the siblings gave a dinner for Jesus. Martha served, Lazarus was at table, and Mary poured a very costly perfume on Jesus' feet and wiped them with her hair, and the whole house was filled with the fragrance. The three teach us hospitality, listening and faith in eternal life. The memorial of Saints Martha, Mary and Lazarus is celebrated on July 29.
joao-maria-vianney:
A boy in times of persecution

John Mary Vianney was born on May 8, 1786, in Dardilly, near Lyon, France, into a devout farming family. When he was only a few years old the French Revolution broke out, churches were closed and priests were persecuted. John Mary's family attended hidden Masses celebrated by priests who risked their lives. He made his First Communion in secret at thirteen, in a house with covered windows. Seeing the courage of those priests awakened in him the desire to become a priest.

The seminarian who could not learn

Only at twenty was he able to begin studying, with the help of Father Balley of Écully. He had enormous difficulty, especially with Latin, and even failed the seminary exams. But his faith and goodness impressed everyone, and Father Balley insisted on defending him. Finally, in 1815, at twenty-nine, he was ordained a priest. In 1818 he was sent as parish priest to Ars, a village of little more than two hundred people, where almost no one went to church.

The Curé of Ars

On arriving, he asked a boy to show him the way and said: "You have shown me the way to Ars; I will show you the way to heaven." He prayed for long hours before the Blessed Sacrament, fasted, visited families, taught catechism and preached simply. He founded a home for orphan girls. Little by little the village changed. Soon people began coming from all over France to confess to him, for he had the gift of reading hearts. In his last years he spent between eleven and sixteen hours a day in the confessional, and tens of thousands of pilgrims went to Ars every year.

Patron of priests

He said that "the priesthood is the love of the heart of Jesus." He died in Ars on August 4, 1859, at seventy-three, worn out from so much service. He was canonized in 1925 and proclaimed patron of parish priests. In 2009, on the 150th anniversary of his death, Pope Benedict XVI dedicated a Year for Priests to him. His memorial is celebrated on August 4.
